# Conductor

> Run graphs of typed Python functions.

A node is a function whose typed signature is its interface. A graph is data: its nodes, each with what is typed into it, and the edges between their outputs and inputs. A registry loads a graph into a `Graph` that reports what is wrong; a `Graph` runs, once per row wherever a list or table arrives, and a run is one value, `Run`, that pauses for a person, resumes and writes itself as JSON. The host declares its own types and nodes.

## Quick Start

One node takes a single value, the other many; that is all iteration is. A list given to an input of one value runs it once per item.

```python
registry = NodeRegistry()


@registry.node("upper")
def upper(text: str) -> str:
    return text.upper()


@registry.node("join")
def join(texts: Series[str]) -> str:
    """Joins every text it is given."""
    return "+".join(texts)


assert upper("a") == "A"  # a node is called like its function

graph = registry.load({            # a graph is data: JSON text, a mapping, or a GraphRecord
    "nodes": [{"id": "upper", "node": "upper"}, {"id": "join", "node": "join"}],
    "edges": [["upper.result", "join.texts"]],
})
assert graph.is_runnable, graph.problems

run = graph.run(text=["a", "b", "c"])  # a list: a row per item; by address, graph.run({"upper.text": ...})
run.outputs                        # {"join.result": "A+B+C"}: what the graph returns, by address
run.results["upper"]["result"]     # ["A", "B", "C"]: ran once per value
run.results["join"]["result"]      # "A+B+C": Series[str] received every value once
```

`make_graph(*nodes, edges=None, values=None, defaults=None)` writes a `GraphRecord`, each node at its version and under its own id (`upper-1`, `upper-2` when one is used twice). With no `edges` the nodes form a chain: each takes its one required input nothing typed in fills from the one output before it (`not_a_chain` otherwise). A chain reads the fields each node declares; a stored graph, or a node whose fields a hook works out, takes `edges=`. With `edges=[("upper.result", "join.texts")]` those are every edge; nothing is matched by name. `values={"upper.text": "x"}` types values in, fixed; `defaults=` the same, open to the caller. The record is loaded against the definitions at the call, each node against the one it was given (two of one id that aren't versions of one node are `duplicate_node_id`), and every fault of what the call said (an address, a value, a type, an edge into a value, a chain it can't draw) is one `InvalidCallError` listing them all; a graph still half drawn (an open input, a cycle) is written, and `graph.problems` says so when it loads.

## Core Concepts

### The Node Contract

`@node("id", version=, title=, description=, category=, tags=, extra=, docs=, policy=, deprecation=, compute_added_inputs=, compute_outputs=, replaces=, upgrade=)` wraps a plain function and returns a frozen, callable `NodeDefinition`; it registers nothing. `@registry.node(...)` takes the same arguments and adds the node to that registry. Only the id is required: the title defaults to the function's name in everyday words, the description to its docstring's first paragraph. `extra` is the host's own JSON about the node, kept and described, never read by conductor.

- Input: `text: str`, or `Annotated[str, Param(title=, description=, widget=, ge=, le=, max_length=, ...)]`. Without a widget an editor shows no control for it: an edge fills it, or a value set in code. A default makes it optional, and is checked against the type where it is written (`default_invalid`). A limit that can't apply to its type (`ge` on a `str`) is refused where it is written (`bound_invalid`). Stacked `Param`s (an alias such as `Annotated[str, Param(widget=TextInput())]` wrapped again with `Param(min_length=1)`) merge as pydantic stacks its fields, the later winning per argument and per limit; a `Param` on a `Series` item is the field's.
- Choices: `Param(choices=[...])`, each a value or a `Choice(id, title)` (from `conductor`), is the one home of a field's choices, carried in its record as `choices`: on a `Literal` field they title its values, one each; on any other they limit what it takes (`not_a_choice`). Each is read as an answer is, strictly from its JSON form and held to the field's limits, so an enum's value or a date's ISO text is a choice. With none, a `Literal` field's choices are its values. An `Ask` gives a question choices the run knows; else a question has its output's. Errors: `choices_invalid`.
- Output: `-> str` is one output named `result`, `Annotated[str, Param(title=)]` says more; a frozen dataclass is one output per field, and `Param(exclusive_group=)` on its fields marks alternatives (at most one holds a value on a row, else `invalid_output`); any other type is one value, a `dict[str, int]` included; with `compute_outputs` the function returns the outputs the hook gives as a mapping by name; `-> None` declares no outputs.
- A value can be blank. If an input's type doesn't say `| None` (`email: str | None`), the node isn't called for that row, its outputs are blank there, and `run.not_called` records the node, row and input. `Series[X]` leaves blanks out, row by row across the series inputs on one table; `Series[X | None]` keeps them. `Series[X] | None` is a list or a blank in place of it, and `Table[R] | None` a table or a blank: `None` given, typed in or its default, a node may return `None` for either, and a list or table never made (its maker had a blank input, or returned `None`) reaches it as `None`; `Series[X] = None` without `| None` is `default_invalid`. Two `Series[X]` inputs reading opposite branches of one decision would lose every row: that is `series_inputs_never_share_a_row`.
- The function returns `SKIPPED` on a branch not taken and raises `Ask(...)` when a person must answer. `Ask` is a `BaseException`, so an `except Exception` in the node lets it through.
- What the run supplies arrives through `FromRun[T]` parameters.
- `@node` checks the function: an `async def`, a parameter with no type, `*args`, `**kwargs` with no `compute_added_inputs`, a dataclass of outputs that isn't frozen, and a field name gone from the next version with no `Upgrade` raise `NodeDeclarationError`, with a `code`.

### Versions and Policies

A newer version names the one it replaces, a `@node` of the same id, and the decorated function is the newest. A definition is one version, and each version names the one before it in `replaces`.

```python
@node("greet")
def greet_v1(name: Annotated[str, Param(title="Name", widget=Textarea())]) -> str:
    return f"Hello {name}"

def _split_name(values: dict) -> dict:
    first, _, last = values.pop("name").partition(" ")
    return {**values, "first": first, "last": last}

@node("greet", policy=Policy(retries=2, retry_delay=0.5, attempt_timeout=10, concurrency=4), replaces=greet_v1, upgrade=Upgrade(rewrite=_split_name))
def greet(first: str, last: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello {first} {last}"

assert greet.versions == (2, 1) and greet.version_of(1) is greet_v1
```

- `Policy(concurrency=1, retries=0, retry_delay=1.0, attempt_timeout=None, retry_on=(), reuse_when_inputs_match=True)`. With `concurrency` 1 and no `attempt_timeout` the node is called in order on the leg's own thread; otherwise on threads, at most `concurrency` rows at once.
- `version=` is one past the version replaced, or 1; a host whose stored graphs have their own numbers names them. `Upgrade(renamed_inputs={old: new}, renamed_outputs={old: new}, rewrite=fn)` goes beside `replaces=`; an input rename carries its value, default and edges in, an output rename the edges out of it and its columns, and `fn` takes and returns what is typed into the node, values and defaults as one map (a default stays one, anything new is a value). It is required only when a field name of the replaced version is gone: a gone input needs a rename or `fn`, a gone output a rename (`upgrade_missing` at the declaration).
- `registry.upgrade(record, node_id, to=None)` moves one node to a version and returns a `GraphRecord`; what it can't do is `InvalidCallError`. Loading never upgrades: a graph saved at an old version runs it.
- `Deprecation(header=, description=, alternative=, migration=)` marks a version going away (`deprecation=` on its `@node`). The `alternative` is an id for a person to read.
- A stored graph is a node too: `node("enrich", title="Enrich")(record)`, with `replaces=` and `version=` as any node, and no `policy` or hook (`not_for_a_graph`), since its nodes run by their own. Loading a graph that uses it puts the stored graph's nodes in its place, on the rows the node runs on; from outside it stays one node (see "The graph record"). From outside its fields go by the names it offers: the open inputs of its first nodes and the outputs nothing inside reads, bare where unique, `node/field` on a clash (`text`, `t/text`).

### Field Hooks

```python
def operand_inputs(count: int) -> dict:          # inputs to ADD; the function takes them as **values
    return {f"value_{i}": float for i in range(count)}


def branch_outputs(names: str, value: type) -> dict:   # all the outputs; value: the type arriving on "value"
    return {name: Annotated[value, Param(exclusive_group="branches")] for name in names.split(",")}
```

Each is a plain function, given per version (`compute_added_inputs=` and `compute_outputs=` on `@node`), run when a graph is loaded, never per row. A parameter names an input and receives its typed value, the declared default included; a parameter annotated `type` receives the type arriving on that input by its edge, `Any` until one does. An input a hook reads is fixed when the graph loads: it takes a typed-in value or the node's default, is never one of the graph's inputs, and a record default there is `default_on_later_node`. If it has neither a typed-in value nor a default, the hook is not called and the node's own problem says why. A hook returns `{name: type hint}`, read like a signature, or `{name: (type hint, default)}` for a field with a default, as pydantic's `create_model` takes one. A hook that raises is the problem `compute_hook_failed` on the node, never an exception; one that raises `NodeError` gives it its message, its `code` as `ctx.error`, and its own `ctx` whole as `ctx.error_ctx`. `graph.describe()` shows each node's fields as its hooks made them.

### Types

Any type pydantic can check and write as JSON travels on edges: `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `date`, `datetime`, a pydantic model, a dataclass or `TypedDict` of your own; a plain class is refused (`type_not_carried`). A subtype lands where its parent is asked for, an `int` lands on a `float`, a `Literal` on a `Literal` holding all its values. A type alias (`type X = ...`, pydantic's JsonValue) is read by its JSON form: what may be written as one of its JSON types lands on it (text, a number or a yes or no on a JsonValue), and it takes a blank as a value when its JSON form may be `null`. A class of your own may declare `id` (the name an editor knows it by, its class name otherwise) and `display_title` as class attributes (`id = "money"`, or annotated `ClassVar[str]`; a field named `id` is each value's own and names nothing), and may declare a classmethod `accepts(source)` that lets values of another type land on it. A subclass of a builtin (`class Text(str)`) is checked as the builtin, then made one. A yes or no never lands on an `int` or `float` input, nor on a host's subclass of one whatever its `accepts` says, by edge (`type_mismatch`), typed-in value (`invalid_value`) or caller (`invalid_input`).

- `registry.types`: every type its nodes declare plus `NodeRegistry(types=[...])`, by id; one id claimed by two classes raises (`duplicate_type_id`). `registry.accepted_as(T)`: the ids a value of `T` may land on.
- `Series[X]`: many values of one type. A plain list to the node and to a type checker; a `polars.Series` returned for one is read as its values, though a checker wants `series.to_list()`. `list[X]` stays one value that is a list.
- `Table[R]`, whose columns a `TypedDict` names by bare type (a column typed `Annotated[...]` is `annotated_extra_unknown`, as its limits would go unread), or bare `Table`: a whole table, a `polars.DataFrame` at run time. To a type checker it is a frame that names `R`: frame methods need no narrowing and a plain `polars.DataFrame` may be returned. A checker shows `R` (`reveal_type`, `assert_type`), but it accepts a table of one row type where another is expected, because the type includes a plain `polars.DataFrame`.

### The graph record

`GraphRecord(nodes=[...], edges=[(from, to), ...])`, stored as `{"nodes": [...], "edges": [["a.result", "b.text"], ...]}`; `NodeRecord(id=, node=, version=1, values=, defaults=, display=)`, empty fields left out when saved. `values`, `defaults` and both records' `display` hold JSON values; `make_graph` writes a Python value as its JSON (a date as its ISO text, an enum as its value, a float that isn't finite as its text, `"NaN"` or `"Infinity"`), so a record equals what its JSON reads back; a record built holding a float that isn't finite is refused. A value with no JSON form, such as a `polars.DataFrame` (give a table as a list of rows), is `invalid_value` at the call. `node` is the id of the node it uses. A node id is not empty and may not contain `.`, `/`, `@` or `~` (`invalid_node_id`).

- From outside, a stored graph used as a node is one node: a caller fills `emb.text`, an author wires `emb.result`, and problems, results, `plan`, `describe()`, `exclusive_groups`, events, waiting rows and a run's `cause` name `emb`, never its inner nodes: it starts once, completes once with the outputs it offers, and says no progress of its own. Where two inner fields share a name, it offers `x/text` with `x` the inner node's id as its own record says it (for a graph embedded in it, that node and the name it offers), so an address of it is `emb.x/text`. It offers what its graph offers loaded alone, fields its hooks add included: `graph.inputs` and `graph.outputs` of that graph, plus each first node's input a hook reads, which the embedding's record may type a value into and a caller never fills. Its inputs stay open to the caller when edges from outside feed only some of them, and each takes a list as its inner input would.
- Edges are a list, kept sorted, so two records differing only in edge order are equal; an edge listed twice stays twice, and loading reports it. Several into one input on rows of one table gather in that table's row order; on different tables, in the order their source nodes appear in `nodes`, then the order a node declares its outputs. An edge is `node.field`, or `node.output.column` for one column of a table. An edge drawn twice is `repeated_edge`; one naming a node the graph doesn't have, at either end, is `edge_names_missing_node`.
- `values`: typed in and fixed; the graph doesn't offer that input to a caller.
- `defaults`: typed in, and the input stays open for a caller to fill. Only an open input of a first node has a caller, so a default elsewhere is `default_on_later_node`: write a value. An input takes an edge, a value or a default, never two (`value_and_edge`, `value_and_default`).
- One value or many: the value decides, never a mark. A list (a JSON array, a Python list or tuple) given to an input that takes one value of a type taking no list (`GraphInput.per_item`) is many values: the node runs once per item, and never sees the difference. A list of one is one row, an empty list none. An input whose own type takes a list (`list[str]`, `Series[...]`, `Table[...]`, `Any`) takes the list as one value; one value given to a `Series` input is a list of one. The same holds for a list typed in as a value or a default: its items are a table under each row the node runs on, and the node runs once per item on each (questions typed into a node that runs per document: once per question per document).
- Two lists never meet uncollected: ten files are ten rows, and which item goes with which is the author's to draw. Two lists a caller gives that reach one node are refused at the call, and two typed into one node (or one typed in under the rows of a list) are a problem of the graph: `lists_not_collected`, in both cases. A `Series` input collects a list whole, wherever its node runs, so a node per contract with a `Series` of appendices gets every appendix on each contract's row; a node that takes the list as one value does too.
- Nothing set: the declared default.
- `display`: the host's own, stored and never read. What a host keeps about the whole graph (a name, a viewport) it stores beside the record.
- An embedding's inputs are filled from outside as any node's are: a value, a default or an edge given from outside takes the place of a default the embedded graph's own record types in.

### Loading

`registry.load(record)` takes a `GraphRecord`, JSON text or a mapping. It never raises for a fault in the graph: each fault is a `Problem` (`type`, `loc`, `msg`, `ctx`) in `graph.problems`, and `graph.is_runnable` says whether there are none.

- The rule: the shape is the call's, what the shape says is the graph's. What doesn't have a record's shape raises `InvalidCallError`, one `invalid_record` problem per fault, at `("record", *where)`, with pydantic's code in `ctx.error`. That covers text that isn't JSON, a key a record doesn't have (`vaules`, or `type` for `node`), a field of the wrong type, and an edge that isn't a pair of addresses.
- The graph keeps its own copy of the definitions it resolved, so a later change to the registry doesn't reach it.
- A graph that embeds definitions loaded for one request loads through a registry of its own: a new `NodeRegistry`, `add_subregistry(shared)`, then `add(*definitions)`. `docs/embedded-graphs.md` teaches it.

- `graph.inputs`: the open inputs of its first nodes (those no edge feeds and no hook reads), by bare name or by address where two share a name. Each is a `GraphInput`: its node's field record (a `FieldDescription`, `name` the input's own) with `address`, `node_id` and `per_item` (a list given here is a row per item); `default` is the record's default, else the node's, as JSON, `None` when `required`. An open first-node input is not a problem; a required input on a later node nothing feeds is `unbound_on_later_node`.
- `graph.outputs`: the outputs of the nodes nothing reads, by address. `graph.plan`: where each node runs, a `RunsOn` whose `mode` is `once` or `per_row` with its `table`, and whose `msg` says it in English. It is the plan of a run given nothing; a run given lists runs on a compile of its own, `run.graph`, whose `plan` says where its nodes ran. `graph.calls_for(file=11)` says before any run how many times each node is called given lists of those lengths (`None` where a node runs on rows another node makes), for an editor's sentence ("with 11 files: 11 calls"). `graph.exclusive_groups`: each node's exclusive groups and their outputs.
- `graph.describe()`: the graph as an editor draws it, a `GraphDescription`: each node's fields as its hooks made them and where it runs, the inputs, the outputs, the problems. Each input of a node says how it is fed on each row the node runs on, its `feed` (a `Feed`: `mode`, `tables`, `under` and `msg`): a `single` value, `per_row` of a table, `copied_down` from a table (a value from rows above) or the `whole_column` of a table (a gather), `under` each row of a table a sibling shares with the node.
- Other codes: `unknown_node`, `unknown_version`, `unknown_input` (a value, default or edge naming an input the node lacks), `unknown_output` (an output, or a column of a table output, the node doesn't give), `type_mismatch`, `invalid_value` (a typed-in value its type refuses), `duplicate_node_id`, `cycle`, `embeds_itself`, `embedded_graph_broken` (a stored graph used as a node has problems of its own, in `ctx`), `rows_not_related`, `hook_needs_value` (a value a hook reads is not typed in), `parameter_name_invalid` (a hook gave a field a name no address can say).

### What a node returns

What a node returns is read strictly by its declared type: a value of exactly that class is taken as it is, a model may come back as a dict, but `"no"` is never a `bool`, `"12"` never an `int`, a date's text never a `date`, and `12.0` never an `int` column. A fault fails that node on that row as `invalid_output` (`ctx`: `name`, `reason`, `errors`, a table's `column`), quoting nothing of the value. A value an edge brings that its source's type doesn't settle (a limit on the input, an `int` into a `float`, a host type's own check) is read by the input as a typed-in value is, and one it refuses is `invalid_input` on the node it reached.

### Rows

A unit is a node on a row; it starts once what it reads exists, so row 1 can finish a chain while row 10 is still being made.

- An output of many values (`Series` or `Table`) makes a table named by it (`split.result`) under the row its node ran on. A row of it is its parent's key plus a number, `(0, 3)`.
- A list or a column on a single-value input runs the node per row; its outputs are columns on those rows. A value from rows above is copied down.
- A `Series[X]` or `Table` input gathers every row under the node's row. It chooses the node's row only when nothing else does: then the node runs once per row of the level right above what it gathers, and with several such inputs, above the shallowest, so none receives a list of one. A gather over a table a branch never made on that row (its maker returned `SKIPPED`) is skipped too, not called on nothing.
- A gather of a sibling table (every keyword of a document, beside each of its invoices) gathers under the row the two share. Several edges on one table into one `Series` input are read in that table's row order, one value per source per row.
- Single-value sources must lie on one path of the row tree. Rows of two different tables never meet by themselves: join them on a key in a node and wire the join (`rows_not_related`).
- Several edges into one single-value input are alternatives, each on its own branch of one decision (outputs sharing an `exclusive_group`, or nodes downstream of them), so a row holds at most one; otherwise `several_edges_into_one_value`. They sit on rows of one table, or `alternatives_on_different_rows`. Whole tables on opposite branches into one `Table` input are the one whose branch ran.
- Each column of a `Table[...]` output is a field at `node.output.column` (`csv.result.email`). A column's name may hold dots, since everything after the second dot is the column.
- Columns and tables wired into one `Table` input are read along one path, a parent's value copied down onto its children's rows. Two columns of one name take their node's id (`name_contacts`).
- A `Table[R]` input receives exactly the columns `R` names. A source that can't give one of them is `type_mismatch` at load.
- A table typed into a `Table` input, or given for one by a caller, is a frame or a list of records; `[]` is a table of no rows. Each column `R` names is read by its own type (a date from its ISO text, a host type from its own text), and other columns are left out. A missing column, or a cell its type refuses, is `invalid_value` when typed in and `invalid_input` when given, with `ctx.column` naming it.
- A stored graph used as a node runs on each row its node runs on, its own reductions folding the rows under that one row.
- `SKIPPED` at a row leaves a gap in the column; above the rows it skips the node.
- `graph.run(max_rows=1000)` is a ceiling on any one table's rows (a typed-in list's are its items times the rows they go under), checked as the rows are made and before any node is called on them. Over it the run stops (`status` `stopped`) with the problem `row_ceiling` (`table`, `rows`, `max_rows`), and `run.resume(max_rows=...)` carries on with a higher one, running nothing again.

### Legs and Asking

One call of `run.resume()` is one leg. A run is its `Run`: every leg returns one, and `status` says how it ended (`complete`, `waiting`, `failed`, `stopped`, `cancelled`, `timed_out`), with `cause`, a `Problem`, for the last four. A node raises `Ask(prompt, choices=, default=, widget=)`: what is asked is what the node returns, so its return type says the answer's shape and how to ask. That row of it and what reads it wait, the rest of the graph runs on, and the leg ends `waiting`:

```python
@registry.node("approve")
def approve(invoice: str) -> bool:
    raise Ask(f"Approve {invoice}?")


approving = registry.load(make_graph(approve, values={"approve.invoice": "INV-1"}))
paused = approving.run()                                 # paused.status == "waiting"
answered = paused.answer(paused.waiting[0], True)        # raises here if wrong; no node runs
finished = answered.resume()
again = approving.load_run(finished.to_json())           # a run is JSON
```

- The return type says how to ask: `bool` a yes or no, `Literal["low", "high"]` one of its values, `str`, `int`, `float`, `date` a value, a frozen dataclass a form of one question per field (a field's default is proposed; one whose default is `SKIPPED` proposes nothing, and left out of the answer is a branch not taken), `Table[R]` a table answered as records, `Series[X]` several, so `Series[Literal[...]]` or `Series[str]` with `choices` is a pick of several. A hook's output types ask the same way.
- `Ask` adds what only the run knows. On a node of one output: `choices=[...]` (each a value, or `Choice(id, title)` to give it a title), `default=`, `widget=` (a widget, as on `Param`). Each has the answer's shape, so on several outputs each goes by output name: `choices={output: [...]}`, `default={output: value}`, `widget={output: widget}`. An `Ask` that doesn't fit the outputs (a default or choice its type refuses, a default an answer couldn't be, `SKIPPED` as a default, no choices or one offered twice, a widget with no JSON form, a name that isn't an output, choices on a table, the one-output form on several) fails the node: `invalid_ask`, with `ctx.reason`.
- Each entry of `run.waiting` is a `Waiting`: `id` (`approve@1~3fa2c0d1`: the node's id, then `@` and each number of its row, `approve` alone for a node that ran once, then `~` and a fingerprint of the question asked there), `node_id`, `row`, `prompt`, `inputs` (what the call received, as JSON) and `questions`, one per output: the field record `describe()` writes (`name`, `title`, `shape`, `type`, `schema`, `required`, ...; a lone output takes the node's title), with `choices` (`[{"id", "title"}]`, from the `Ask` or a `Literal`), `default` and `widget`.
- `run.answer(unit, value)` answers one row; `run.answer({unit_id: value, ...})` answers several in one call. It returns a new run, and nothing runs until `resume()`.
  - A node of one output is answered with its value, a node of several with a mapping by output name. In the mapping, a question with a default may be left out, and so may one with a blank-taking type and no choices. Of an `exclusive_group`, exactly one is answered; the others are branches not taken.
  - Each answer is read strictly from its JSON form: `true`, not `"yes"` or `1`; `3`, not `"3"`; a date as its ISO text. It is checked against its question before anything runs.
  - Every fault is refused at once, and nothing is answered: `invalid_answer` (`ctx.waiting_id`, `ctx.reason`, and `ctx.question` when it is about one), `not_waiting` for a unit not waiting, and `answer_stale` (`ctx.current`, the id waiting there now) for an id whose row has held another question since, as after `run.again` moved the rows.
  - An id without its `~` part names the place alone and answers whatever waits there. A node that asked is not called again for that row.
- `run.to_json()` is the whole run. It names the graph it is of by `graph.fingerprint`: the record's nodes, versions, values, defaults and edges, not `display`.
- `graph.load_run(saved)` refuses a save of another graph as `state_of_another_graph`: an edited graph starts a new run, and `edited.with_inputs(..., earlier=old_run)` lends it the old run's work for the nodes the edit left as they were. Then it reads the save back and checks it against the graph. A row its makers never made, a row listed twice, a missing output, or a table whose column length isn't its row count is `state_unreadable`, with `ctx.at` the `node.output` (or `node.output.column`) where. So is a save of the wrong shape (a key missing, a status no run has, a `max_rows` below 1), with `ctx.at` the dotted place in the save (`units.upper.states`) and `ctx.reason` pydantic's message; a mapping with no JSON form is one at `the run`. A float that isn't finite comes back the float wherever the save marked it, inside a tuple or a model's field included.
- A value with no JSON form is `state_unwritable` at `to_json`, naming where too.
- A parameter typed `FromRun[T]` receives the value of `T` from `run.resume(from_run={T: value})` or `graph.run(from_run=...)`. A value of a subclass of `T` fills it too, keyed by its own class: a test double, a host's own session. A missing one is `from_run_missing` (naming what was given), several that fit `from_run_ambiguous`, at the call. `FromRun[T]` is the whole parameter's type, never inside `| None`, a list or an output: anywhere else a caller could fill it (`from_run_misplaced`).

### Running again

`run.again(**changed)` runs with changed inputs, the rest as before, and reuses what it can (`run.with_inputs(**changed)` is the same run not started, to `resume()` or `stream()`, as `graph.with_inputs` is to `graph.run`): a unit whose inputs match what an earlier unit of its node received takes that result, even if its row moved, and the node isn't called. Answers are reused the same way.

```python
@registry.node("send")
def send(contact: str) -> str:
    return f"sent to {contact}"


sending = registry.load(make_graph(send))
contacts = ["ida@a.dk", "bo@b.dk"]
first = sending.run(contact=contacts)                     # two mails
second = first.again(contact=[*contacts, "eva@c.dk"])     # one row added: one mail
```

- The key is what the unit is about to receive, by content, plus the node's version, its code (the function's own bytecode and constants, as a saved run records it), its fields and the rows it runs on. A `FromRun` value is not part of it.
- Identical rows take the earlier ones in row order, the k-th to the k-th, whatever thread finished first: a third identical row is new work, and with one identical row taken out, which earlier answer stays goes by that order, not by who answered. An answer, or a question still waiting, is reused only under the same rows above it, so two documents' identical lines keep each document's answers when the documents move. A row still waiting goes on waiting at its new row, asked nothing new.
- `again` carries the work the run before it carried and didn't use, while its node still has a row waiting, so an answer survives an edit and its revert; when a node finishes, its leftovers are dropped, so an edit undone two runs later calls that row again.
- `run.forget("node", ...)` is a run of the same inputs that calls those nodes again (an embedding's id forgets its nodes), and a node below that then receives what it did before is reused: a host checks access again this way.
- `Policy(reuse_when_inputs_match=False)` is for a node whose result depends on the world, not its inputs (a file read by its path, today's exchange rate): `again` calls it on every row.
- `node_complete.reused_units` says how many rows were reused.

### Retries and Timeouts

Retries live on the node's `Policy`, per unit.

- Only `ExternalFailure` retries: raised by the node, or a class in `Policy.retry_on` (`external_failed`). Anything else is `execution_failed` or the node's own `NodeError` code, run once. A `NodeError` other than `ExternalFailure`, an `invalid_output` and an `Ask` are never retried, even when `retry_on` names a class they derive from, such as `Exception`.
- Attempt `n` waits `retry_delay * 2 ** (n - 1)` and emits `node_retry`.
- `Policy.attempt_timeout` bounds one attempt: the unit fails with the code `timeout`, final; the thread is not interrupted.
- `run.resume(timeout=60)` ends the leg `timed_out` (a `timeout` or `checkpoint_every` that is not a finite number of seconds above 0, a `bool` included, is `invalid_timeout` or `invalid_checkpoint_every` at the call, and a `max_rows` of `True` is `invalid_max_rows`); `run.stream(cancel=asyncio.Event())` ends it `cancelled` when set, and so does leaving the loop once the stream is closed: Python closes an async generator left early only when it is collected, so hold it with `async with contextlib.aclosing(run.stream()) as events:` and loop over `events`. Either way the calls already made finish and are kept, so resuming repeats none of them.

### Errors

The classes are exported from `conductor`. What is wrong is always one record, `Problem(type, loc, msg, ctx)`: on `graph.problems`, on `node_failed` and `run.cause`, and in `InvalidCallError.errors()`. Its `type` is a stable code (see "Problem and error codes"); a node failure's `loc` is `(node_id, *row)`, a graph problem's `(node_id, field)`.

```
NodeDeclarationError    a node or registry declared wrong, at import; a TypeError, with code
InvalidCallError        a call was given what it cannot act on, every fault listed
NodeError               a node's own failure: message, code, ctx
└── ExternalFailure         retried
```

A failed unit ends the leg `failed`, its problem on `run.cause`: nothing more starts, the calls already on a thread are waited for (each as far as its `attempt_timeout`) and kept, so resuming doesn't repeat them. A call that can't be acted on raises `InvalidCallError`, whose `errors()` lists a `Problem` for every fault, and nothing changes. Running a graph with problems raises it too, listing them. A failure never quotes a value the run handled: a node's exception other than a `NodeError` goes to `logging.getLogger("conductor")` and only its class name reaches `ctx`.

### Events

`async for event in run.stream():` yields frozen models from `conductor.events`, the union `Event` on `type`; the call is checked before anything is yielded. `run_start` is always first and `run_end` always last. The leg runs on a thread of its own, so a slow node never holds the event loop. `run_end` writes `status` and `cause`, the run's `Problem` when it failed, stopped, was cancelled or timed out (`null` otherwise), so a client sees why a leg ended (a `row_ceiling` cause carries `rows` and `max_rows`): `event.run` is for the host to save, and holds every value; no event carries a node's values. An event writes itself as JSON: `event.model_dump(mode="json")`.

| Event | Carries |
|---|---|
| `node_start`, `node_skipped` | `node_id` |
| `node_progress` | `node_id`, `done`, `total` (`None` until every row exists); at most four a second per node |
| `node_complete` | `node_id`, `rows`, `not_called` (how many rows a blank kept it from), `reused_units`; the values are in the run (`run.results`) |
| `node_retry` | `node_id`, `row`, `attempt`, `retries`, `delay`, `cause` |
| `node_failed` | `node_id`, `cause` (a `Problem`) |
| `unit_waiting` | `unit` (a `Waiting`) |
| `run_start` | `waiting` |
| `run_checkpoint` | `run` (status `running`, or how a stopped leg stopped), which it does not write; only with `stream(checkpoint_every=seconds)`, at most that often and once when a leg is stopped with calls on threads |
| `run_end` | `status`, `cause`, and `run`, which it does not write |

### Saving a graph

Records are frozen pydantic models. `GraphRecord` and `Problem` round-trip through JSON; a `Run` writes itself with `to_json()` and reads back with `graph.load_run`.

```python
record = make_graph(upper, join)
text = record.model_dump_json()
assert GraphRecord.model_validate_json(text) == record
```

### The Palette

`NodeDefinition.describe()` is a `NodeDescription`, a pydantic record (`id`, `version`, `versions`, `title`, `description`, `category`, `tags`, `extra`, `docs`, `deprecation`, `is_graph`, `policy`, `inputs`, `outputs`, `takes_added_inputs`, `computes_outputs`), each field a `FieldDescription` (`name`, `title`, `shape`, `required`, `type`, `json_schema` written as `schema`, `columns`, `default`, `choices`, `description`, `widget`, `exclusive_group`; a key it doesn't have is `None`; a `Param`'s limits are in `schema`, as `minimum`, `maxLength` and the like, and its title and description are the field's own, never repeated there). `registry.describe()` is a `RegistryDescription`: `nodes` and `types` (each `id`, `title`, `accepted_as`). A stored graph's palette entry lists the fields it offers only in `registry.describe()`, which holds the nodes its graph uses; its definition's own `describe()` lists none. `graph.describe()` is a `GraphDescription`. Each is a host's response model as it is; `model_dump(mode="json")` writes it.

## API Reference

Four public modules: `conductor`, `conductor.widgets`, `conductor.events` and `conductor.testing`. Each lists its names in `__all__`; import from nothing else.

### conductor

- Nodes: `node`, `NodeDefinition`, `Upgrade`, `Policy`, `Deprecation`, `Param`, `FromRun`, `Series`, `Table`
- In a node: `SKIPPED`, `Ask`, `Choice`, `NodeError`, `ExternalFailure`
- Registry: `NodeRegistry(*, category="", tags=(), extra=None, types=())` (`@registry.node`, `add(*definitions)`, `replace(definition)`, `remove(node_id)`, `add_subregistry(registry)`, `filter(predicate)`, `load(record)`, `upgrade(record, node_id, to=None)`, `in`, `[]`, `len`, iteration over the definitions, `types`, `accepted_as`, `describe`). A node entering a registry takes its defaults: tags add up, outermost first; the node's own `category` and `extra` keys win. A second node under one id raises; a subregistry is copied in when added.
- Graph: `GraphRecord`, `NodeRecord`, `make_graph`, `Graph`
- A run: `Run`, `Waiting`
- Errors: `NodeDeclarationError`, `InvalidCallError`, `Problem`, `PROBLEM_CODES`

### Running

- `graph.run(inputs=None, /, *, max_rows=None, from_run=None, timeout=None, **by_name)`: one leg from the start; its `Run`. A pause or failure is a `status`.
- `graph.with_inputs(inputs=None, /, *, max_rows=None, **by_name)`: a `Run` with the inputs checked and not started; a name it doesn't offer (`not_offered`), a required one left out (`missing_input`), one given by both its name and its address (`input_given_twice`), a value its type can't read (`invalid_input`), two lists that meet (`lists_not_collected`) or a `max_rows` below 1 (`invalid_max_rows`) raises `InvalidCallError`, every fault at once.
- `run.resume(*, max_rows=None, from_run=None, timeout=None)`: the next leg. `run.stream(...)`, the same arguments and `cancel=`: the leg's events.
- `run.answer(unit, value)` or `run.answer({unit_id: value})`, `run.with_inputs(inputs=None, /, *, max_rows=None, **by_name)` (a run carrying this one's work, to resume or stream), `run.forget(*node_ids)` (a run of the same inputs that calls these nodes again, carrying the rest, to resume or stream), `run.again(...)` (the same, resumed; takes `from_run=` and `timeout=` too), `run.to_json()`, `graph.load_run(saved)`, `graph.calls_for(lengths=None, /, **by_name)` (each node's calls given lists of these lengths, before any run; a name it doesn't offer or one given by both its name and its address raises `InvalidCallError`).
- `run.results`: every node's outputs so far, by node id: one value for a node that ran once, a list in row order for one that ran per row, `None` where a row has none. `run.outputs`: narrowed to `graph.outputs`, by address, on a `complete` run only (`run_not_complete` otherwise). `run.waiting`, `run.not_called`, `run.status`, `run.cause`.

### Problem and error codes

A `Problem`'s `type` is a stable code, and a host translates by it, filling its sentence from `ctx`. `PROBLEM_CODES` is every code conductor itself writes, for a test that pins your translations to it. A code that isn't in it is a node's own, from a `NodeError`. `docs/problems.md` (https://github.com/syv-ai/conductor/blob/main/docs/problems.md) has every code, the declaration codes and `check_registry`'s among them, each with its message, an example and the fix.

### conductor.widgets

Frozen models with a `type`, and a host subclasses `Widget` for a control of its own; loading and the engine never read one. `title`, `description` and the limits of a value (`ge`, `gt`, `le`, `lt`, `multiple_of`, `min_length`, `max_length`, `pattern`) belong to the `Param`, and a value outside its limits is refused. An untitled field reads as its name in everyday words. No type has a default widget. A widget on a `Param` or an `Ask` is anything with a JSON form; one with none (a class passed bare) is `widget_not_json` at `@node`.

| Widget | For | Options |
|---|---|---|
| `TextInput` | one line of text | none |
| `Textarea` | several lines | `rows` |
| `Dropdown` | one of the field's choices, from `Param(choices=)` or a `Literal`'s values | none |
| `NumberInput` | a number typed in | `step`, `integer_only` |
| `Slider` | a number between the `Param`'s `ge` and `le` | `step` |
| `Switch` | on or off | none |
| `DatePicker` | a date | `initial` |
| `FileUpload` | uploaded files | `accept`, `max_size_mb`, `multiple` |
| `ListInput` | a list typed by hand | none |

### conductor.testing

`check_registry(registry, /, *, examples=None, expected_failures=None, from_run=None)` is one test a node package or host runs in CI: `assert check_registry(registry, examples={"upper": [{"text": "hi"}]}) == []`.

- It returns every problem at once as `Problem`s, `loc` `(node_id, version)`. For `waiver_not_needed`, and for `example_for_no_node` given without a version, `loc` is `(node_id,)`.
- A body is called only for a node given an example, once per example, through the engine as a graph of that one node. `(id, version)` keys an older version's examples, and `from_run={T: value}` gives every example's `FromRun` values, as `graph.run` takes them.
- The checks are `hook_failed`, `needs_example`, `upgrade_broken`, `changed_its_inputs`, `run_failed`, `pause_untested`, `example_for_no_node` and `waiver_not_needed`; `docs/problems.md` says what each means and how to fix it. These codes are `check_registry`'s, not in `PROBLEM_CODES`.
- `expected_failures={"id:code": "why"}` accepts a failure in the test; one that no longer fails is reported.

### conductor.events

Every event record: `Event` (the union on `type`), `RunStart`, `NodeStart`, `NodeProgress`, `NodeComplete`, `NodeSkipped`, `NodeFailed`, `NodeRetry`, `UnitWaiting`, `RunEnd`.

## Serving Runs

The core has no HTTP in it. `syv-conductor-providers` has `conductor_providers.fastapi.run_router(store=, registry=, caller=)`, a FastAPI router mounted with `app.include_router(...)`: `GET /nodes`, `POST /load`, and a run you start, follow, read, answer, resume, run again and cancel by id, from any worker; `docs/serving-runs.md` is its guide. The host writes the `conductor_providers.fastapi.RunStore`, six async methods over one row per run whose every change is a compare-and-set on `rev`, and a FastAPI dependency for the caller, a class or a function with a return annotation, whose type is kept on each run. `registry=` may be a function of the caller, for a registry per tenant. A node is given a way to connect, never a connection, because it runs on another thread. An answer claims the run at the revision it read. A lease, renewed while a leg runs, lets another worker resume a dead worker's run from its last `run_checkpoint`. A deploy cancels its legs and hands them back. Answers sent while a leg runs wait on the run and are applied when it ends.

## Project Structure

```
packages/
└── conductor/src/conductor/            __init__, widgets, events, testing: the four public modules
    ├── about/                          this document
    └── _internal/                      everything else; import nothing from here
```

## CLI Reference (this document)

```bash
python -m conductor.about                 # full text
python -m conductor.about sections        # section slugs
python -m conductor.about rows            # one section (prefix or substring)
```

Or `from conductor.about import get_content, list_sections, get_section`.
